title: Consultant Explains the Pyramid Principle
transcript: Ah, the notorious pyramid principle. You may love it, hate it, or perhaps you've never even heard of it, but there's a more than likely chance you've already seen it used in a presentation. In this video, I'll discuss what the pyramid principle is, how it's used in major consulting firms, and why it's so useful. (Upbeat music) Simply put, the pyramid principle is just a structured form of communication where you start with the main point and then move through the supporting details of that main point. So, for example, let's say you asked your friend who their favorite basketball player is. She might say something like: I like players who can play in different positions, but who can also score a lot of points and be team leaders. So, I really like LeBron James. Now, observe the structure of this response. That's reason number one - she likes players who can play in different positions - reason number two - she likes players who can score a lot of points - and reason number three - she likes players who can be team leaders. And then the answer comes right at the end. And this is a perfectly normal and acceptable way to answer a question. But let's say she used the pyramid principle, in which case she might say something like, "My favorite player is LeBron James because he can play in different positions, scores a lot of points, and is a team leader." So, did you notice the difference between the two? In the second example, she gets straight to the point and then follows through with her reasoning to that main point. And that makes everything much easier for me, as a listener, because when I know she 's talking about LeBron James, it's much easier to follow her reasoning. Now, let's take this example a step further and say that she's going to map this out for you on paper. But that's not all; She will add a few more details to her argument. So, we arrive at the main point: LeBron James is your favorite player, after the three reasons we stated earlier. And now we have some details for those reasons. And if you didn't already know, this is where the information resembles a pyramid, with the main point at the top and the details organized logically and structurally below. But there's something much more important happening here. Each box is intended to capture the main point of all the boxes below it. So, for example, this box here provides a nice summary statement for the two below it. And of course, if you look at our top box, you'll see a summary of the entire pyramid. At this point, it's worth pausing to note that the whole idea of ​​the pyramid principle came from a woman named Barbara Minto, who was a consultant at McKinsey in the 1960s. So, if you really enjoy studying logical structure and communication, her book is a great read. It's called the "Pyramid Principle," and we'll certainly include a link to it in the description below. Okay, so we put our pyramid in place. Now let's make this a little more practical. Let's say your friend now wants to convey her point of view, so she'll give a full presentation about it. All she needs to do is organize these ideas onto her own slides to form the outline of the presentation, also called a storyboard. Notice how her first slide presents the main idea in summary, and then she goes into detail in the following slides. This is the pyramid principle in action, and it's exactly how leading consulting firms apply it in their client presentations. There are so many advantages to this approach, but one of them is that it is more efficient. If your friend had waited until the end to tell you that her favorite player is LeBron James, your brain would have had to go back and think about the different reasons she had already given you and try to evaluate each reason after the fact. But if she gives you the answer beforehand, you can evaluate each reason she presents and then decide if it's something you agree with. In a real presentation setting, this approach has the added benefit of saving time because if, for example, you tell an executive your main point at the beginning, you can spend your time on the parts of that main point with which he or she disagrees. instead of having to watch each part of the presentation just to figure out the main point at the end. It 's also much more flexible. Since the first slide contains the main idea, she could simply present that slide and you would understand what she is trying to tell you. Or, if she had more time, she could present the first slide, then the three main supporting points, and that would be it. So, of course, if she had unlimited time, she could give the full presentation with all the details. But in each of these scenarios, the overall message remains unchanged. That's because you have more details. So, one final reason is that this makes the argument easy to follow. The goal of your presentation is to make it as easy as possible for your audience to understand your main message. And the pyramid principle helps someone easily see what your main point is and how you arrived at each of your conclusions. In the world of consulting, it's important to back up all your claims, and the pyramid principle provides a structured way to do that. So there you have it: a brief explanation of the pyramid principle.
